slides.title: Beat 1
slides.body:
Welcome back.
In last video we formalized the set,
Today we formalize subset.
The textbook says A is a subset of B when every element of A is already in B.

slides.title: Beat 2
slides.body: Here is the key idea, just like last time. Subset is not a new container. It is a proposition about two sets you already have. B is not built from A.
slides.notes:

def Set (α : Type u) := α → Prop

Turn:
as before

slides.title: Beat 3
slides.body: Quick reminder, this is the same Mathlib file from the last clip. You still have def Set, Set dot Mem, and the Membership instance. Subset is going to build right on top of these.
slides.notes:
Lean:
def Set (α : Type u) := α → Prop

namespace Set
  protected def Mem (s : Set α) (a : α) : Prop :=
    s a

  instance : Membership α (Set α) :=
    ⟨Set.Mem⟩

Turn:
as before

slides.title: Beat 4
slides.body: First, protected def Subset. It takes s one and s two, both of type Set alpha. So it relates two sets, it does not create one.
slides.notes:
Lean:
namespace Set
  -- …Mem and Membership from last clip…

  protected def Subset (s₁ s₂ : Set α) :=

Turn:
as before

slides.title: Beat 5
slides.body:
The body is for all a, a in s one implies a in s two.
That is exactly the textbook rule.
The double braces around a make it instance-implicit, so Lean again infer the element type for you.
slides.notes:
Lean:
namespace Set
  protected def Subset (s₁ s₂ : Set α) :=
    ∀ ⦃a⦄, a ∈ s₁ → a ∈ s₂

Turn:
as before

slides.title: Beat 6
slides.body:
Notice the in symbols here.
They still come from Set dot Mem in the last video.
So subset is just putting 2 of membership condition together in an implication.
slides.notes:

as before

slides.title: Beat 7
slides.body:
Now the registration, the same idea as Membership before.
we implement the typeclass LE on set so that we can have use the notation >= on 2 sets.
And again, the angle brackets make Set.Subset the implementation of the only method in typeclass LE.
slides.notes:
Lean:
  protected def Subset (s₁ s₂ : Set α) :=
    ∀ ⦃a⦄, a ∈ s₁ → a ∈ s₂

  instance : LE (Set α) :=
    ⟨Set.Subset⟩

Turn:
as before

slides.title: Beat 8
slides.body:
Then the typeclass HasSubset registers the subset symbol itself.
But it use the notation from LE that we just implemented.
So both <= notation and subset notation desugars to Set.Subset def of 2 sets
slides.notes:
Lean:
  protected def Subset (s₁ s₂ : Set α) :=
    ∀ ⦃a⦄, a ∈ s₁ → a ∈ s₂

  instance : LE (Set α) :=
    ⟨Set.Subset⟩

  instance : HasSubset (Set α) :=
    ⟨(· ≤ ·)⟩

-- A <= B and A ⊆ B desugars to Set.Subset A B

Turn:
as before

slides.title: Beat 9
slides.body: So that is Lean's modelling of subset. One def for the rule, two instances to register the ordering and the symbol, and a theorem tying the notation to the for-all form.
slides.notes:
Lean:
-- Mathlib source: mathlib4/Mathlib/Data/Set/Defs.lean
namespace Set
  protected def Subset (s₁ s₂ : Set α) :=
    ∀ ⦃a⦄, a ∈ s₁ → a ∈ s₂

  instance : LE (Set α) :=
    ⟨Set.Subset⟩

  instance : HasSubset (Set α) :=
    ⟨(· ≤ ·)⟩

end Set

Turn:
as before
